generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, progressing means running these three habits together whenever the work gets hard, not reaching for one at a time. A setback becomes information, which feeds the self-belief and learning motivation to keep going, which you aim at a mastery goal. Across a term, those small rounds add up into steady progress.
generatedProse.worked-example: Two students meet the same hard module. One reads a poor early mark as proof they cannot do it, loses heart, and sets only a target mark to chase. The other reads the mark as information, builds confidence by mastering one part at a time, and sets a goal to build a lasting skill. By the end of term, the second student's work is far stronger, because the three habits worked together.
generatedProse.summary: Progressing is most useful as one continuing practice, not three separate tricks. You meet a setback with a growth mindset, keep going on self-belief and learning motivation, and aim that effort at a mastery goal, then carry it into the next task. It is the three working together, round after round, that moves your learning forward.

check.body: A student gets a poor mark on an early essay. They read the feedback as showing what to work on, build their confidence by improving one weak area at a time, and set a goal to get better at structuring an argument. By the end of term their essays are stronger. What does this show?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first essay, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next essay.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using feedback to plan the next piece of work feeds it straight back into your learning, closing the loop and starting the next round stronger. That is the cycle working as it should.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student did with the feedback, and what improved as a result.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Acting on feedback feeds your next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay was stronger. The mark on the first essay cannot change, but the feedback still shapes what comes next.

_items.text: That the three habits worked as one practice: a growth response, self-belief and learning motivation, and a mastery goal, each feeding the next across the term.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three ran together, round after round, and the work improved.

_items.text: That the first poor mark was a fair verdict on their ability.
_items.feedback: The point is the opposite: the student treated the mark as information, not a verdict.

_items.text: That only the final essay mark matters, not what came before it.
_items.feedback: What came before is the point. The habits across the term made the later work stronger.

_items.text: That setting a goal alone was enough, with no change in mindset or effort.
_items.feedback: The goal worked because a growth response and real effort sat behind it.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
